mcqs.question: What is the key granularity mismatch in NAND flash that shapes SSD write behavior?
options: Reads happen per-block while writes happen per-page
Reads, writes, and erases all happen at exactly the same granularity
Reads and writes happen at page granularity, but erases happen at the coarser block granularity, which holds many pages
Writes happen per-cell while reads happen per-block
mcqs.explanation: The page-vs-block mismatch (fine-grained read/write, coarse-grained erase) is the defining structural fact of NAND flash. The other options invert or flatten this mismatch incorrectly.

mcqs.question: Why can't a flash page simply be overwritten in place the way a hard disk sector can be?
options: Because flash pages are physically read-only after their first write
Because overwriting a page would corrupt the SSD's file system metadata
Because flash controllers are too slow to process individual page writes

Because clearing charge back to the erased state requires a high voltage applied to the entire containing block, not a single page, so a page must be erased at block granularity before it can be rewritten
mcqs.explanation: The physical asymmetry — charge can be added to a page but only cleared at block granularity — is why in-place overwrite is impossible. Pages aren't permanently read-only, controller speed isn't the limiting factor, and file system metadata is a separate software-layer concern.

mcqs.question: Why are SSD random reads fast while SSD writes involve more hidden work than they appear to from the application's perspective?
options: Reads have no mechanical cost and reach any page in roughly the same time, while a write can't overwrite in place — it must be redirected to a fresh erased page with the old one marked stale for later reclamation
Reads and writes are equally simple; the perceived difference is a myth
Writes are slow because they must be encrypted before being stored on flash
Reads are fast only because they are always served from a DRAM cache rather than the flash itself
mcqs.explanation: The read/write asymmetry comes directly from flash's erase-before-rewrite constraint, which forces writes into a redirect-and-reclaim pattern invisible to the caller. Encryption isn't the cause of write complexity, and reads are fast due to flash's electrical (non-mechanical) nature, not exclusively DRAM caching.

mcqs.question: Why have consumer SSDs largely moved to TLC and QLC flash despite their lower endurance compared to SLC/MLC?
options: TLC/QLC actually have higher endurance than SLC in modern manufacturing processes
Storing more bits per cell increases capacity per unit of silicon, and the cost-per-gigabyte advantage outweighs the endurance trade-off for typical, read-heavy consumer workloads
TLC/QLC are required by the NVMe protocol specification
SLC and MLC flash are no longer manufactured at all
mcqs.explanation: The capacity/cost benefit of more bits per cell is what drove the consumer market to TLC/QLC, since typical usage doesn't stress endurance limits as heavily. TLC/QLC have lower, not higher, endurance than SLC; NVMe is a protocol, not a flash-type mandate; and SLC/MLC still exist in enterprise/niche products.
